and the remedy cannot be refused solely on the basis that substitute performance is 
possible. In one illustrative case, the Dijon Court of Appeal ordered the perform­
ance of a contract for the sale of computer equipment in circumstances where the 
equipment that had originally been supplied did not conform to specification. The 
vendor was required to provide a replacement.43
Building contracts are also specifically enforceable. In many cases builders have 
been ordered to rectify work that does not conform to contractual specification.44 
By way of example, the remedy was granted in respect of a contract to construct a 
chalet.45 The Cour de cassation has also quashed a decision refusing to order the 
demolition and reconstruction of buildings which, in breach of contract, were built 
out of conformity with contractual specification.46
The possibility that an order for specific enforcement might require a high de­
gree of supervision does not seem to have caused the same concern in France as in 
England, with potential difficulties in ensuring compliance passing without men­
tion in the literature on the topic. This can also be inferred from the willingness of 
French courts to order specific enforcement both of building contracts and where 
the effect of the order is to require the defaulting party to carry on a business. For 
example, in a case arising out of the oil crisis in the 1970s, an airline discontinued 
flights on a route between two towns which had been rendered financially onerous 
because of significant increases in the price of aviation fuel. This amounted to a 
breach by the airline of a contract with the Chamber of Commerce of one of the 
towns that the route would be kept open. The Cour de cassation affirmed the de­
cision of the Besançon Court of Appeal to order specific enforcement. Despite 
the change in global economic circumstances, the fulfilment of the obligation re­
mained possible.47
(ii)  The specific enforcement of negative promises
The breach of a negative promise is equally widely restrained in France. In one case, 
for instance, the Cour de cassation quashed the refusal by the Lyon Court of Appeal 
to order that leased premises, which had been altered in breach of a negative obli­
gation not to modify them during the demise, be restored to the condition in which
